rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four actually different desks to choose from, then tells them exactly what proof will make each desk care. Its strongest line, "Monzo's second US attempt starts invite-only, without the banking license it failed to get last time," is a real reporter-shaped story; B's "A UK challenger bank turned its first annual profit — then went back to America" is good, but it drifts into category sermon with "category thesis was wrong." B is competent, but two of its three angles are cousins in the same P&L trench coat.
gaps_in_A: "Nine million UK customers, zero in the US" invents a cleaner fact than the update gives. Invite-only launch does not equal a verified zero-customer baseline.
"Monzo reached profitability at home, then immediately spent it" overstates causality. The update gives profitability and US launch, not a disclosed spend decision or timing link.

"European challenger banks stalling in the US" may be true, but it is outside the supplied facts. A flags the proof need, which saves it, but the angle still needs real comparative sourcing before pitching.
gaps_in_B: "category thesis was wrong" is too grand for one company posting one annual pre-tax profit. That is not a thesis-killer; it is a question worth testing.
"A UK challenger bank turned its first annual profit" and "Monzo's first profitable year, by the numbers" both circle the same profit/CAC/US-expansion tension. Pick the sharper one or merge them.
"by the numbers" promises a data piece while the actual pre-tax profit figure, CAC, US targets, revenue, and baseline are missing. That headline is writing checks the facts cannot cash yet.
B underuses the invite-only fact. It mentions it in the license angle, then leaves the consumer/access story on the table.
